title: Michel Foucault
keyWorks: The Use of Pleasure and The Care of the Self (1984)
summary: Foucault investigated how power works not only through prohibitions but through “norms”: schools, hospitals, questionnaires and grades quietly teach us what to be. He showed that much of what seems “natural” in us has a history — which means it could have been otherwise. In his late work he turned to the ancient “care of the self”: to how a person can give shape to their own life.
onEmotions: Foucault did not build a theory of emotions, but he teaches us to ask our feelings an unexpected question: not only “what’s wrong with me?” but also “where did I get this yardstick?” Many of our shames, anxieties and feelings of inadequacy are traces of “normalization” — society’s habit of comparing everyone to a norm. This view lifts part of the burden: not everything that hurts is your personal fault. And the late Foucault adds that you can treat your feelings as material for “technologies of the self” — calm, attentive work on your own life, without self-punishment.

anxiety.text: Epictetus advised testing every impression the way a money-changer tests a coin: is it counterfeit? Foucault saw this as one of the ancient "technologies of the self". Anxiety is an honest reaction to a world that expects a great deal of you. Foucault described another image too — Bentham's panopticon, a prison where the inmate can't see the guard and so watches himself, just in case. This is how "disciplinary power" works: it doesn't need to punish constantly; it is enough that we feel we might be seen and judged. Part of anxiety is an inner guard: an exam that never ends, even when no one is watching. It is a trace of how schools, offices and feeds are built. When you notice whose gaze is built into your anxiety, it becomes information about the world rather than a verdict on you.
anxiety.practice: Take one anxious thought and test it like a money-changer tests a coin: whose stamp is on it — yours, or someone else's gaze? Say the answer out loud.

fear.text: At the start of "History of Madness" the "ship of fools" sails by: medieval towns, according to Foucault, put unwanted people on a boat and sent them away down the rivers. He showed that the line between the "normal" and the "dangerous" shifts over history: different eras pushed different people beyond it. Fear is often intelligent: it notices danger before we manage to name it. But many of our fears — of being "not right", of falling outside the norm, of being excluded — were absorbed along with these lines. Foucault insisted that power is never total; at every point a response is possible. Fear doesn't mean you are helpless. It can show you where the line runs — and a line you can see can be thought about, not only feared.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: what am I afraid of — the event itself, or who I'll be taken for if it happens? Write down both answers.

quote.text: Where there is power, there is resistance.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: The Will to Knowledge (The History of Sexuality, vol. 1), 1976

sadness.text: The Greeks kept "hypomnemata" — notebooks in which they copied out what they had read and lived through, so as to gather themselves from these fragments. The late Foucault studied such "technologies of the self" very closely. There was no rush in them to fix a mood — only careful attention. Today the unspoken norm is to be positive and productive, and sadness looks suspicious beside it. Foucault called "normalisation" the way society divides states into healthy and deviant and gently nudges everyone towards the middle. The very rush to "fix" sadness is part of that normalising pressure. Sadness can be given a place in your day: not driven out but listened to and written down — and then it becomes part of your own text rather than a deviation from someone else's.
sadness.practice: Keep a "hypomnema" for one evening: write down three sentences about your sadness and one line from a book or song that resonates with it.

grief.text: "To make live and to let die" — this is how Foucault described the formula of modern power, which is busy with health, life expectancy, efficiency. Death has meanwhile become the most private, almost hidden moment of existence, pushed out of shared space. If it seems to you that people around you expect you to "pull yourself together quickly", this is not only their callousness but a feature of a culture that has little room for loss. Grief is one of the deepest experiences, and no one has the right to set it a deadline. You can give it back its place yourself. The ancient "technologies of the self" that Foucault studied are practices a person creates for themselves without waiting for permission: rituals, letters, reflections, conversations with those close to them.
grief.practice: Create a small ritual of remembrance today — not "the proper way" but the way you need: light a candle, walk a familiar route, play this person's favourite music.

loneliness.text: Seneca wrote his letters to Lucilius as if they were sitting side by side, and Foucault saw this correspondence as one of the main forms of "care of the self". He stressed that care of the self was never a solitary business — students talked with teachers, friends helped each other see themselves. Loneliness truly hurts, and behind it lies a need for others. Foucault also showed that disciplinary power "individualises": it distributes people into separate places, files, rows in a table — each apart, each comparable. Part of loneliness is not your personal failure but an effect of a world that has sorted us into cells. Reaching for others when you are lonely is the very essence of care of the self.
loneliness.practice: Write a short letter — as Seneca did to Lucilius — to someone you'd like to talk with about life. You don't have to send it.

anger.text: "The art of not being governed quite so much" — this is how Foucault, in the lecture "What Is Critique?", defined the critical attitude. Anger is a legitimate signal: something has touched your boundaries or your sense of justice. Foucault wrote that discipline produces "docile bodies" — useful, convenient, predictable people. Anger is often the first bodily sign that something in you refuses to be merely convenient. This is not a call to destruction, nor a reason to shame yourself for being angry. It is rather an invitation to turn anger into a precise question: against which exact way of treating me am I protesting? Once the answer is found, anger stops being a vague heat and becomes knowledge of what matters to you.
anger.practice: Walk for a couple of minutes, feeling your steps, and as you go finish the sentence: "I don't want to be treated like this: …" What lies behind that "like this"?

quote.text: …the art of not being governed quite so much.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

shame.text: Foucault describes how the "examination" was born in the schools and barracks of the eighteenth century: everyone is observed, compared with everyone else, entered in a register, and their deviations noted. He called this "normalising judgement". Shame is one of the most painful feelings, and often it is the feeling of having failed an examination on the norm. Foucault also showed that our culture has taught people to seek "the truth about themselves" in what is most secret and shameful, as in confession. But a norm is a historical invention, not a law of nature: it has a date of birth and authors. This doesn't cancel your actions and your responsibility, but it lets you separate what you actually did from someone else's yardstick that you carry inside.
shame.practice: Name the norm before which you feel ashamed and ask: how old is it, who set it, whom does it benefit?

quote.text: The soul is the prison of the body.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

guilt.text: Every evening, when the light was put out and his wife fell silent, Seneca went over the day: where was I wrong, what did I do well? Foucault analysed this exercise in detail and noticed the key point: Seneca looked at his lapses not as a judge but as an administrator checking the accounts. Guilt says that you care how your actions affect others — it is a valuable feeling. Christian confession, as Foucault describes it, taught people to decipher their sinfulness endlessly. The aim of the ancient "technology of the self" is not to punish oneself but to adjust one's conduct. Guilt can become not an endless trial of yourself but a calm inventory: what happened, what I can put right, what it teaches me.
guilt.practice: Go over one situation "as an administrator": what I wanted, what happened, what I'll do differently — without using the word "bad".

envy.text: "An entrepreneur of himself" — this is how Foucault, in the lectures "The Birth of Biopolitics", described the person of the neoliberal era who constantly invests in his "human capital". In such a world envy is almost built into the design of life: we compare our "capitals" non-stop. Foucault showed that disciplinary society is a society of ranks: tables, grades and ratings make everyone visible and comparable. Envy is a very human feeling, and there is nothing monstrous in it; all this merely explains why it is so sharp. The late Foucault proposed a different measure: life as a work with its own style, not as a place in someone else's table. Envy can hint at what you want, but it needn't decide by which scale you live.
envy.practice: Imagine the ranking in which you are currently losing, and tear it up in your mind like a useless register. What remains of your desire once the table is gone?

emptiness.text: "Why should the lamp or the house be an art object, but not our life?" Foucault asked in one of his late interviews. He spoke of an "aesthetics of existence": for the ancient Greeks ethics was not a code of rules but work on oneself, like an artist's work. Emptiness and apathy can be very heavy. Sometimes they arrive when ready-made forms of life — met expectations, "proper" roles — stop filling you. This is not necessarily a breakdown; it may be an unpainted part of the canvas. Foucault proposed no grand plans: technologies of the self are small, repeated practices through which a life gradually takes shape. Emptiness doesn't need to be stuffed with whatever comes to hand. You can ask which small actions give you even a faint sense of your own style.
emptiness.practice: Do one small thing today not "because you have to" but as a brushstroke on your life-as-a-work: move an object, wear something you like, walk down a different street.

quote.text: But couldn’t everyone’s life become a work of art?
quote.author: Michel Foucault

confusion.text: Foucault begins "The Order of Things" with laughter: in Borges, a certain "Chinese encyclopedia" divides animals into "belonging to the Emperor", "drawn with a very fine camelhair brush" and "having just broken the water pitcher". This laughter, Foucault writes, shatters the familiar order of thought. Being at a loss resembles such a moment: familiar landmarks stop working, and the seams become visible. Foucault's method, "genealogy", shows that what seems eternal and natural — from the notion of "normality" to our ideas about ourselves — has a history and could have turned out otherwise. He called critique work "at the limits", where we test what in us is necessary and what is contingent. You needn't rush to find a new final formula for yourself; you can stay in this gap and see what can be seen from it.
confusion.practice: Write down one thing about yourself that you considered "natural" and now doubt. When, and from whom, did you pick it up?

quote.text: Do not ask who I am and do not ask me to remain the same.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

fatigue.text: "Before you govern others, take care of yourself," Socrates tells the young Alcibiades — and with this dialogue Foucault begins the history of "care of the self". Tiredness and burnout are not laziness but a living being's reaction to overload. Foucault described in detail how discipline organises time: timetables, the principle of "not losing a minute". Later this logic spread: the neoliberal "entrepreneur of himself" now optimises his whole life. Burnout is the place where the body refuses to be endlessly useful. Ancient care of the self, by contrast, was not self-optimisation: it included solitude, walks, conversations, reading, pauses — time that owes nothing to anyone. Rest, seen this way, is not a reward for productivity but the very practice of relating to oneself.
fatigue.practice: Find five minutes in today that won't be "used" for anything. Notice how hard it is not to fill them.

boredom.text: "Discipline and Punish" opens not only with an execution but also with the timetable of a Paris house for young prisoners: rising, prayer, work, meals — every minute scheduled. Foucault called this "disciplinary time". Boredom is not a whim but a signal: it often appears when we live inside a form we didn't choose and repeat someone else's routine. The late Foucault spoke not of great revolutions but of "practices of freedom" — small shifts in everyday life through which a person begins to decide for themselves how to live. Boredom offers a pause in which the form becomes visible. There's no need to seek strong sensations at once; it is enough to notice where the timetable has become your prison, and shift it a little.
boredom.practice: Do one habitual thing slightly differently — by another route, in another order — and notice what has changed in how it feels.

joy.text: The ancient Greeks, as Foucault showed in "The Use of Pleasure", asked not "is this pleasure permitted?" but "how can it be used beautifully and with measure?" Pleasures were for them neither sin nor commodity but material for the art of living. Joy needs no justification — neither by usefulness nor by merit. In "The Will to Knowledge" Foucault proposed relying not on imposed schemes of "correct" desire but on "bodies and pleasures" — on what is directly experienced. A joy that no one grades and that serves no purpose is a small territory of freedom from normalisation. It doesn't need to be displayed or turned into productivity. It can simply be lived.
joy.practice: Notice one pleasure of today that serves nothing and is judged by no one. Don't tell anyone or post it — let it stay yours alone.

love.text: How can people be together — share their time, meals, leisure, grief, knowledge, confidences? Foucault asked this in the interview "Friendship as a Way of Life" and believed the answers were still to be invented. He showed that what is most intimate in us is organised too: love is surrounded by networks of advice, institutions and ideas telling us how to love "correctly". Tenderness and love are among the most precious experiences, even when they don't fit understandable frames. If your tenderness doesn't match the template — too quiet, too strange, not "leading" anywhere — that is not a mistake. It is a space where you yourself give shape to your bonds.
love.practice: Do one thing for someone you love for which your relationship has no ready-made name: a small ritual, a shared joke, a walk "just because".

gratitude.text: Socrates' last words — "We owe a cock to Asclepius" — Foucault, in his final lecture course, read not as a complaint that life is a disease but as gratitude: friends and conversation had cured him of false opinions. Gratitude is a warm and important feeling. Foucault thought a great deal about "parrhesia" — courageous frank speech, when someone tells another the truth at the risk of the relationship. Among the most precious gifts are those brought by people who dared to be honest with us. There is another thought in his spirit too: gratitude shouldn't be turned into yet another norm — "keep a gratitude journal or there's something wrong with you". Then it becomes discipline. Living gratitude is free: it comes by itself and demands no report.
gratitude.practice: Recall someone who once told you a hard truth. If you can, tell them today what you're grateful for — that is a small parrhesia too.

hope.text: "Not everything is bad, but everything is dangerous," Foucault said, "and then we always have something to do": his position leads not to apathy but to active engagement. Genealogy shows that what seems unchangeable arose in history, and so can change. Foucault was sceptical of grand promises of final liberation, but his philosophy is in its own way very hopeful. Hope, then, is not waiting for someone to come and fix everything but the knowledge that the world is not closed and there is still room in it for your step. It doesn't require optimism about everything at once; one small place where you can do something is enough.
hope.practice: Name one thing that seems unchangeable right now. When and how did it arise? What small part of it could you shift?

quote.text: My point is not that everything is bad, but that everything is dangerous… If everything is dangerous, then we always have something to do.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

nostalgia.text: In the essay "Nietzsche, Genealogy, History" Foucault mocked the search for a "pure origin" — a golden beginning after which everything went wrong: the past, in his view, was never whole and flawless. Foucault the historian was not nostalgic at all. But he valued the past for something else: its strangeness shows that the present is not the only possible one. Nostalgia is a tender feeling: we long for what once held us. It can be read not as longing for a lost paradise but as knowledge that life can be arranged differently. Then the past becomes not a place you can't go back to but a hint at what can be invented here and now.
nostalgia.practice: Recall what exactly you love about the past and choose a small piece of it — a dish, a habit, a route. Don't bring it back; reinvent it today.

craving.text: "Who is master here — me or the desire?" This, according to Foucault, is how the ancient Greeks posed the question. In "The Use of Pleasure" he showed that their ethics was built not on prohibitions but on "enkrateia" — self-mastery, the ability not to become a slave of one's pleasures. A sharp "I want it right now" can sweep over you completely, and there is nothing shameful in that. What mattered to the Greeks was not shame but measure and timing. Freedom for them meant not the absence of desires but that desire doesn't decide for you. The wave of craving needn't be cursed or obeyed at once. It can be watched the way one watches weather: it rises, peaks and subsides.
craving.practice: When the wave comes, set a timer for five minutes and simply note how its strength changes: stronger, the same, weaker.

addiction.text: A file, a diagnosis, a "case" — Foucault showed how society turns a person into a category that starts to obscure everything else. He reminded us that a person is never reducible to a label. If life has long revolved around one thing, that is exhausting — and it is not a moral failure. The late Foucault, studying the ancient "technologies of the self", described notebooks in which Greeks and Romans jotted down thoughts and observations in order to give shape to their lives gradually, day by day. This was neither confession nor self-punishment but patient work. The way out of a long-standing circle is not one heroic leap but many small practices of freedom. They are often easier to do together with others — in a mutual-help group, for instance.
addiction.practice: Start a small notebook and write one observation about today in it — without judgement, as a note to yourself.

hangover.text: Confession, for Foucault, is one of the great machines of Western culture: we are used to extracting the truth from ourselves as if under interrogation. The morning after is heavy for body and soul: anxiety, shame, gaps in memory, and the inner interrogation is right there. But in his lectures on "technologies of the self" Foucault showed another way. Seneca went over his day not as a judge passing sentence but as an administrator who checks the accounts and calmly notes what to do differently next time. You can take the administrator's position: not wring guilt out of yourself but note what happened and what will be useful tomorrow. This doesn't cancel responsibility, but it removes the self-trial. Right now you can be gentle with yourself.
hangover.practice: When it gets a little easier, write two lines: "What happened" and "What I'll take note of" — in the tone of an administrator, not a judge.

euphoria.text: In the essay "What Is Enlightenment?" Foucault recalls Baudelaire: modern man, for Baudelaire, is not the one who goes off to discover himself but the one who tries to invent himself. A burst in which everything seems possible is a vivid experience, and you can simply enjoy it. Foucault described philosophy as testing the limits imposed on us and looking for the possibility of going beyond them. Euphoria is a bodily experience that limits can move and the world is open. At the same time the late Foucault, following the Greeks, valued measure and long "work on oneself" more than brief flashes. So euphoria can be not only lived but kept: remember which possibility it showed you, without making big decisions on its wave.
euphoria.practice: Write down in one sentence which limit seems movable to you right now. Not as a plan, but as an image.

crash.text: The Greek word "askesis" meant not heroics or deprivation but exercise, and Foucault, studying the Stoics, stressed exactly this sense: calm daily practices that help one live through both highs and lows. A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid evening — can be very hard, and it is not your fault. In "Discipline and Punish" Foucault showed how society trains us to an even, controlled rhythm. Against this background any drop is easily read as a breakdown. But you can ask: whose norm is it that demands you always be even and cheerful? The "comedown" is not a verdict but a time for small, unhurried actions.
crash.practice: Choose one simple act of care for your body — going outside, washing your face, making tea — and do it slowly, as an exercise.

panic.text: "Docile bodies" — this is what Foucault called bodies that discipline has taught to be manageable, composed, always under control. That is why the moment when your heart pounds, your breathing falters and it seems something irreparable is about to happen is doubly frightening: the body slips out of control. Foucault didn't write about panic attacks, but the late Foucault turned to ancient "care of the self", which included care of the body — attention to breathing, routine, simple exercises. Not suppression, but careful attention. In panic you can stop fighting your body and look after it, as you would someone close. Such a wave usually rises and subsides within a few minutes.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and feel the support. Place a palm on your belly and tell your body "I'm here," making each out-breath longer than the in-breath.

dread.text: "The Order of Things" ends with an image: man may be erased "like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea". Foucault was speaking not of people perishing but of the fact that our idea of "man" is a recent invention that may give way to another. Horror before the abyss, the question "what is it all for?" — this is a deep experience, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Foucault showed that it is precisely finitude, limitation, that makes human beings able to know and to ask. The late Foucault added: the meaning of life is not given in advance, but it can be created by treating one's own life as "a work of art". The question "why" is not proof of meaninglessness but the start of the work. The answer is built from small deeds, relationships, attachments.
dread.practice: Watch something moving for a couple of minutes — clouds, water, trees outside the window. Then name one small thing from today that was even a little dear to you.

fomo.text: In Bentham's panopticon the few watch the many; Foucault showed how this gaze made its way into schools, factories, hospitals. Today we live in a reversed panopticon: the many watch the many, we constantly see other people's lives and compare our own with them. Foucault called this mechanism "normalisation": the perpetual comparison of everyone with an average measure. The feeling that everyone lives more interestingly and you're not where you should be is very common, and it's not only about you. It is a consequence of a machine of visibility that runs round the clock. Hence the relief: what you are shown is not the whole truth about other lives but a shop window, carefully arranged for the gaze.
fomo.practice: Notice whose life you compare yours with most often, and ask: "What am I seeing — a life, or a shop window?"

sleepless.text: Foucault's "The Care of the Self" opens with Artemidorus' dream book — an ancient work on how to interpret dreams, and so on how people listened to their nights. Sleepless hours when thoughts won't let go can be very lonely. Foucault showed how modern society built disciplinary time: schedules, deadlines, the use of every minute. Sleep, too, became part of this logic: it must be properly "replenished" so that you work well tomorrow. If we carry Foucault's thought further, night-time anxiety is often the voice of the same norm: "you won't get enough sleep, you won't cope". That doesn't make sleeplessness your fault. The night needn't be turned into an exam: even quiet rest without sleep is still rest.
sleepless.practice: Tell yourself: "Right now I don't have to get anything done." Write your anxious thoughts on a sheet, one line each, and set it aside until morning.

betrayal.text: For the Greeks, as Foucault showed in his last lectures on "parrhesia", telling a friend the truth meant taking a risk: opening up, saying something that could harm you yourself. Such frankness is possible only where there is trust. Betrayal wounds deeply because it breaks that unspoken pact in which you opened up and took the risk. Foucault also wrote about "friendship as a way of life" — about bonds people create themselves, without ready-made rules. Relationships are always a creation, never a guarantee. Your pain is the trace of what you truly invested in this relationship, and your capacity for frankness remains with you. Foucault would add: to risk frankness is already the act of a free person.
betrayal.practice: Say one honest sentence about your feelings today to someone you still trust. Your capacity for frankness is yours; it hasn't been taken away.

jealousy.text: Power, for Foucault, is present in all relationships, even in love, and that isn't necessarily bad: in living relationships it is mobile, a game in which both are free. He distinguished it from a "state of domination" — when the game freezes and one person tries to control the other completely. Jealousy is agonising: the fear of losing someone close clenches everything inside. It can be understood as a wish to stop the moving game and fix it forever, because uncertainty is frightening. This is a very human wish, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. But Foucault would remind us: the liveliness of a relationship consists precisely in both people remaining free. Fear is part of that price.
jealousy.practice: Write down what exactly you want to "lock in" in this relationship, and what the other person's freedom means to you.

resentment.text: Genealogy, Foucault wrote after Nietzsche, looks not for a noble origin but for the accidents, errors and coincidences from which what seems eternal was put together. Try looking at an old grudge this way. If you carry it, you really were hurt. It seems part of you, as if it had always been there and always will be. But it has a history: when it appeared, what fed it, how it changed. This view doesn't require forgiving or forgetting. It only lets you see the grudge as a story rather than as fate — and then it can have a continuation that you write.
resentment.practice: Draft a short "genealogy" of your grudge on paper: when it appeared, what fed it, how it has changed over time.

heartbreak.text: Our society, Foucault observed in the interview "Friendship as a Way of Life", offers a strikingly poor set of recognised forms of closeness — essentially the couple and the family. So when a couple breaks up, it feels as if the whole world is collapsing: there seem to be no other forms for love and connection. A break-up is an enormous loss, and this pain deserves to be acknowledged. But Foucault called for inventing new relationships — friendships, alliances, attachments for which there are no names yet. The end of a relationship is not the end of your capacity for closeness. Love and connection can take many forms, and some of them are already in your life; they're just not usually counted as the main ones.
heartbreak.practice: Call or meet someone today with whom you have a "not the main kind" of relationship: a friend, a neighbour, a sister. Spend some time in that form of closeness.

impostor.text: "Maybe the target nowadays is not to discover what we are but to refuse what we are," Foucault wrote in "The Subject and Power". The fear of being found out at any moment affects many people, including those who are doing perfectly well. Foucault showed how the "examination" works: observation and assessment turn a person into a "case" with scores and marks. We have grown used to the idea that our worth must be constantly confirmed by someone above us. Impostor syndrome is life inside an endless exam, where any moment may turn out to be a test. Perhaps you don't need to prove that you are "real". It is enough to do what you do.
impostor.practice: Ask yourself: "Who is this imaginary examiner?" Describe them out loud in one sentence — and notice that you don't have to sit their exam.

quote.text: Maybe the target nowadays is not to discover what we are, but to refuse what we are.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

self_hatred.text: In "History of Madness" Foucault tells of Tuke's asylum in York: the chains were removed there, but the patient was taught to feel a constant gaze and guilt upon himself — the guard moved inside. The inner critic resembles such a guard. When the inner voice is merciless, living with it is very hard, and you deserve gentleness. The late Foucault noticed something else too: the Christian tradition taught people to search themselves for sin and renounce themselves, while ancient "care of the self" was careful work in which a person treats themselves as someone to be looked after, not punished. Self-hatred is not the truth about you but one historically formed way of relating to oneself. There are others.
self_hatred.practice: Say the inner critic's sentence out loud and ask: "Is this the voice of a guard, or of someone who cares for me?" Then say the same thought in the voice of care.

helplessness.text: "Where there is power, there is resistance," Foucault wrote in "The Will to Knowledge". Power, in his view, is not concentrated entirely somewhere at the top but dispersed through a multitude of small relationships — in families, at work, in conversations. This means that not everything has been decided for us. The feeling of being powerless to change anything can be very heavy, and it deserves to be taken seriously. But even where big changes are out of reach, "practices of freedom" remain — small chances to act differently: in how you speak, whom you spend time with, how you treat yourself. You are not all-powerful, but you are not entirely powerless either: between these extremes lies the space where freedom lives.
helplessness.practice: Do one small thing today that is in your power — even if it seems insignificant: say "no", move a meeting, leave the house ten minutes earlier.

procrastination.text: "Exhaustive use of time" — this is what Foucault, in "Discipline and Punish", called the ideal of discipline: not a single minute should be lost, a person should always be productive. We have absorbed these demands so deeply that any delay feels like failure, and it's easy to call yourself lazy. If we carry Foucault's thought further, procrastination is sometimes the body's quiet resistance to this regime rather than a vice of character. This doesn't mean the task needn't be done. But you can ease the pressure: instead of forcing yourself heroically, try a small exercise, as the Stoics did — one action, without self-punishment. The Stoics knew that a small step repeated day after day changes more than a heroic leap.
procrastination.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and do the smallest part of the task. When it rings, you are free to stop.

uprooted.text: The ship, Foucault wrote in the lecture "Of Other Spaces", is the heterotopia par excellence: a place without a place, floating between shores. Life after a move resembles such a space: you are no longer there and not yet here. When the ground has gone from under your feet — a move, emigration, the loss of a familiar world — it is a deep loss, even if the decision was right. But this position holds a special knowledge too: you see that the norms of both the old and the new world are not laws of nature but historical habits. This doesn't cancel the longing, but it gives you the freedom to choose what to take with you from both worlds. Foucault himself spent several years away from France — in Sweden, Poland, Germany, Tunisia.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new place and find your own "heterotopia" — a corner where you feel at least a little at home: a bench, a shop, a square. Spend a couple of minutes there.

overload.text: Seneca called "stultitia" the state of a mind that darts from one thing to another and can settle on nothing; Foucault saw it as the opposite of "care of the self". The endless flow of information and feeds really is exhausting. In "The Will to Knowledge" Foucault made an unexpected discovery: modern power works less through prohibition and silence than through an "incitement to discourse" — to endless talking and confessing. We are made to speak, show and consume what others have said all the time. Overload is not your inability to keep up but a consequence of a set-up in which the flow must never stop. The Stoics chose: to read little, but attentively. You can allow yourself not to know everything.
overload.practice: Copy out from today's flow one thought that will really be useful to you, and close the rest.

unreality.text: "Am I asleep?" Descartes asks himself in the "Meditations", sitting by the fire in his dressing gown; Foucault analysed this passage closely in "History of Madness". The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real can be frightening, and it deserves gentle treatment. Foucault showed that the line between "normal" and "strange" experience is not eternal: different eras drew it differently, and those who went through something unusual were often simply silenced. Your experience is part of a long human experience of doubting reality. It doesn't make you alien or "wrong". It can be spoken about rather than hidden — and the very act of saying it often helps you come back.
unreality.practice: Describe out loud three things around you as concretely as possible: colour, shape, temperature.

awe.text: In "The Masked Philosopher", an interview Foucault gave anonymously, he dreamed of curiosity in the old sense of the word: a readiness to find what surrounds us strange and remarkable, to break away from the familiar and look at the same things differently. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience, and you can simply let it fill you. Foucault was also interested in "limit-experiences" — moments in which a person briefly steps beyond themselves. Awe is one form of such experience: familiar measures disappear, and the world seems unexpected again. In these minutes your norms and judgements step back for a while. Nothing needs to be added to this moment; it is enough to let it last.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what filled you with awe, without taking photos or searching for words.

relief.text: Foucault described the examination as one of the main techniques of power — and probably understood why the bell after the last exam sounds so sweet. We live under constant observation and assessment: reports, deadlines, other people's expectations. Relief often comes at exactly the moment when the exam is over and the guard's gaze has turned away for a while — and it deserves to be noticed. You can see how much strength went into holding on. Relief is not only a pleasant feeling but also a clue: it shows what exactly was pressing on you. And the late Foucault, drawing on ancient "care of the self", would remind you: rest and recovery are not a reward for work but part of how a person builds their life.
relief.practice: Take a long out-breath and straighten your shoulders, as after an exam you've passed. Name silently what exactly has just let go.

calm.text: "Claim yourself for yourself" — with these words Seneca opens his letters to Lucilius, and Foucault saw in them one of the central ideas of "care of the self". In the lectures "The Hermeneutics of the Subject" he examined in detail how ancient philosophers — Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius — practised "withdrawal into oneself". This is not flight from the world but the skill of returning to oneself in the midst of affairs, finding an inner place where one can rest. A person belongs not only to their duties but also to themselves. Calm is a precious state, and you can simply stay in it. Your calm is not idleness but a small practice of freedom. It needn't be justified by usefulness or results.
calm.practice: Sit for a minute, noticing your breath, and tell yourself in Seneca's words: "Right now I am claiming myself for myself."

inspiration.text: What is thinking worth doing for? Foucault answered in the introduction to "The Use of Pleasure": for the chance "to get free of oneself", to think differently from how one thought before. Inspiration — the moment when thought flows by itself and you want to create — is exactly such a getting free. Foucault spoke of life as "a work of art" and of an "aesthetics of existence" — the skill of giving shape to one's own life. Inspiration is not a rare gift of the chosen few but a moment when this ability suddenly becomes tangible: you see that it is possible to think and live differently. It needn't take the form of a result at once. It is enough to give it room and keep it while it's fresh. Foucault admitted that he wrote in order to change himself and not to think the same thing as before.
inspiration.practice: Note down what has come, as it is, without editing — as a note in your own notebook.

quote.text: There are times in life when the question of knowing if one can think differently than one thinks, and perceive differently than one sees, is absolutely necessary if one is to go on looking and reflecting at all.
quote.author: Michel Foucault

schadenfreude.text: A table, a ranking, a register — Foucault showed that modern society is built as a system of constant comparison that puts everyone in a place relative to everyone else. He called this "normalising judgement". In a world where everyone is ranked all the time, someone else's failure involuntarily feels like a small advance in your own table. Schadenfreude is an uncomfortable feeling, but almost everyone has it, and in itself it doesn't make you a spiteful person. It is partly an echo of this system, not only a personal trait of yours. Understanding this doesn't justify cruelty, but it removes needless shame. And it prompts a question: which competition am I taking part in without having chosen to?
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: in which ranking did someone else's failure make me "better"? Who invented that ranking, and when?

contempt.text: In 1656 the General Hospital opened in Paris, and, by Foucault's reckoning, one in every hundred inhabitants soon found themselves inside — the poor, the mad, vagrants. He called this "the great confinement": the reason of the modern age defined itself by separating off and locking up what it considered unreasonable. Contempt works in a similar way: we assert ourselves through those we place lower and gain a feeling of superiority and safety — I'm not like that. This doesn't make you bad, but it shows that contempt may be less knowledge about the other than a way of holding on to one's own "norm". A useful question: what boundary in me is this contempt guarding, and what am I afraid of if it disappears?
contempt.practice: Name a quality you despise in someone else. Then ask: what would I fear if I discovered it in myself?

disgust.text: "Since when, and why, has this been considered disgusting?" Foucault's genealogical question can be asked even of the most bodily of feelings. He showed that much of what seems naturally "normal" or "abnormal" has a history: norms take shape and change. Disgust is a strong feeling, and it often has its reasons. But it is partly learned: society teaches us what to regard as unclean, dangerous, indecent. It helps to distinguish disgust that protects you from real harm from disgust that repeats other people's norms. This applies especially to disgust at oneself: it often speaks in the voice of a culture that taught us to be ashamed of the body, of weakness, of deviation. That voice can be heard — and disagreed with.
disgust.practice: Ask your disgust: "How do I know this is disgusting?" Write down whose voice you heard in the answer.

revenge.text: "Discipline and Punish" opens with a description of the execution of Damiens in 1757 — a spectacle in which the vengeance of power fell upon a body. Foucault showed how society gradually gave up such spectacles, but not punishment: it became quieter and went deeper. The wish for revenge is a natural reaction to injustice; it is a wish for power, a wish to regain the strength that was taken from you. But in the preface to Deleuze and Guattari's "Anti-Oedipus" Foucault warned: do not fall in love with power. In revenge the offender still holds you: you are still living by their script. Perhaps real strength lies not in punishing but in freeing yourself from the role they imposed on you.
revenge.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly was taken from me — strength, dignity, voice? Name one way to take it back without harming anyone.

quote.text: Do not become enamored of power.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: Preface to the English edition of Deleuze and Guattari’s Anti-Oedipus (1977)

anger_at_loved.text: "The microphysics of power" was Foucault's name for the way power runs not only through the state but also through the warmest relationships — between spouses, between parents and children. Yet power relations are not evil in themselves: in any closeness people influence each other, argue, give way. The trouble comes when the moving game freezes into domination. Anger at those close to us is an ordinary, if painful, part of closeness; afterwards we are often ashamed of it. But it frequently signals that something in the relationship has frozen: someone always decides, someone always gives in. This is not a reason to cause pain but a reason to notice the game and speak about it calmly.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger subsides, ask yourself: what has frozen in our relationship? Tell your loved one in one calm sentence, starting with "It seems to me that we…".

ambivalence.text: Confession, and then medicine and psychology, according to Foucault, taught Western people to believe that one real "truth" lies hidden deep inside them — about their desire, their feelings, themselves. Hence the tormenting question: "What do I really feel for this person?" Mixed feelings — love and irritation, tenderness and weariness at once — are a very common state. The question of the "real" feeling becomes a trap if it demands a single final answer. Your relationship is not a riddle to be deciphered but a living practice that you create. Both sides of your feelings can be true, and you can work with both. Foucault distrusted the demand "confess who you really are" in general.
ambivalence.practice: Instead of asking "what do I really feel?", ask yourself a different question on a walk: "How do I want to build this relationship today?"

guilty_relief.text: How long should mourning last, what should it look like, what is permitted in it? Foucault taught us to see that such questions have unspoken norms, and these tell us what it is "normal" to feel. Relief after an ending — a break-up, the end of a loved one's long illness — often arrives together with guilt. It doesn't cancel your love. Shame about relief is often shame before a norm, not before real people. The norm demands a single pure feeling, but life is more complicated. If you spent a long time caring, worrying, carrying the weight, relief is a natural response. It doesn't contradict love; it tells of how much you endured. The norms of mourning are not written by those who did the night-time caring.
guilty_relief.practice: Name the "rule" that says relief is out of place right now. Where does it come from? Does it fit your actual story?

indifference.text: Joy at a celebration, tears at a funeral, agitation at the news — if we carry Foucault's thought further, feelings have norms too, and we constantly check ourselves for compliance. Sometimes you're untouched by what "should" touch you, and that is frightening. Fear of one's own indifference is often fear of failing the exam for being a "normal" person. But feelings aren't obliged to follow a timetable. Indifference may be tiredness, a defence, a temporary pause. The late Foucault wrote about "care of the self" — an attentive rather than punishing attitude towards oneself. You can simply notice your state without turning it into a verdict. Indifference today, something else tomorrow: feelings have their history too.
indifference.practice: Replace the question "why don't I feel what I should?" with "what do I need right now?" — and answer it.

escape.text: A garden, a library, a fair, a ship — Foucault called such places "heterotopias", "other spaces" where the usual order seems suspended. The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — often appears when life feels like a cage. Foucault described society as a network of institutions — schools, factories, offices — that order people's time, bodies and behaviour. The wish to escape can be a response to this pressure, a signal that you are tired of living by someone else's routine. Sometimes real change is needed; sometimes it is enough to find your own heterotopia. Either way it helps to ask: which routine exactly do I want to get away from? A heterotopia can be very small: the library on Saturdays, a park bench, another city for a weekend. It doesn't cancel ordinary life, but it shows that the order of things can be different.
escape.practice: Find one "other place" in your week — where the routine is different for at least an hour. How could you spend time there more often?

forbidden_attraction.text: For the Greeks, Foucault wrote, desire was not a sin to be confessed but a force one had to learn to handle wisely: the question was not "what is forbidden?" but "how do I want to live with this force?" Later the Christian tradition made desire an object of confession and suspicion. Being drawn to someone unavailable or "not the one" is disorienting. In itself it is neither a crime nor a diagnosis, and not yet an act. It is part of your life, which you can approach as material for reflecting on what kind of life you want to build. The Greeks would ask not "am I guilty?" but "what will I do with this force?"
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down what this attraction says about your life right now: what is missing from it, or what is asking to come out?

quote.text: Freedom is the ontological condition of ethics. But ethics is the considered form that freedom takes when it is informed by reflection.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: Interview “The Ethics of the Concern for Self as a Practice of Freedom” (1984)

social_anxiety.text: Velázquez's "Las Meninas", with whose analysis "The Order of Things" begins, is a painting about gazes: the painter looks at us, we look at him, and in a mirror at the back the king appears, whom we cannot see. Foucault thought all his life about how the gaze works. His panopticon is a prison where inmates don't know whether they are being watched right now, and so they begin to watch themselves. Fear of people and their judgement can be paralysing: we constantly feel an evaluating gaze upon us and become our own guards. Social anxiety is not a personal defect but partly an echo of this system. The guard inside is not you but a voice that can be noticed and named.
social_anxiety.practice: When it seems everyone is looking, glance around and count how many people are actually looking at you right now. Notice the real gazes, not the imagined ones.

uncertainty.text: Every morning the Stoics calmly imagined possible misfortunes — "premeditatio malorum" — so as to meet them prepared; Foucault described this exercise as one of the "technologies of the self". He saw such practices as a way for a person to shape their own attitude to life rather than wait to have it shaped. Uncertainty wears you out: it's unclear what will happen. Foucault always stressed that what exists now is not eternal; everything has a history and can change. Uncertainty is also openness. The future is not written in advance, and there is room in it for your freedom. The Stoic exercise is not about fear but about calm: if the difficulty comes, you will already have an answer.
uncertainty.practice: Calmly, without hurrying, imagine what might go wrong, and answer silently what you would do in that case. Then let the picture go and return to what you were doing.

waiting.text: In a letter to his teacher Fronto, Marcus Aurelius describes an entirely ordinary day in detail: his sore throat, the grape harvest, what he talked about with his mother at dinner; Foucault analysed this letter as an example of care of the self. Waiting — for an answer, results, news — is agonising partly because time seems to belong to someone else, to whoever decides. Foucault showed how disciplinary society manages time: deadlines, queues, stages of inspection. Ancient philosophers took their time back: they kept notebooks, wrote letters, practised reflection. Waiting can be turned, at least in part, into your own time — not empty but filled with what you have chosen yourself.
waiting.practice: Send someone a short letter in the spirit of Marcus Aurelius — about the most ordinary things in your day, and not a word about what you're waiting for.

regret.text: "Do not ask who I am and do not ask me to remain the same," Foucault wrote in the introduction to "The Archaeology of Knowledge". Regret over what you did or didn't do can gnaw at you for a long time, as if you had remained forever the person who made that mistake. Foucault distinguished two ways of looking at one's past. One is tied to confession: searching oneself for sin, confessing and bearing guilt. The other is ancient: every evening Seneca reviewed the day not as a judge but as an administrator, so as to notice what hadn't worked and do better tomorrow. Regret is useful when it helps you act differently, and tormenting when it turns into an endless trial of yourself. You are free to choose the path of care of the self.
regret.practice: In the evening, review the day as a calm administrator: what didn't work, and what will you do differently tomorrow? No verdict on yourself.

longing.text: In the essay "Self Writing" Foucault shows that for ancient authors a letter to a friend was more than news: it let one feel the presence of the absent one, almost like a gaze. Seneca told Lucilius that a letter brings "real traces" of a friend. Missing a particular person can be acute: you lack their voice, their habits, their presence. Longing is a form of connection that continues in absence. It can not only be endured but also carefully kept: written down, remembered, spoken aloud. A letter turns the pain of absence into a conversation that goes on. Ancient friends wrote to each other not only about important things — about the weather, minor ailments, books they had read — and the person themselves lived in these small things. Your longing, too, can find a form: not silencing it but giving it a voice.
longing.practice: Write a short letter to this person — you don't have to send it. Tell them what happened today.

world_pain.text: "Do not think that one has to be sad in order to be militant, even though the thing one is fighting is abominable," Foucault wrote in the preface to "Anti-Oedipus". Hurting for the world — over hard news, wars, injustice — can be very heavy, and it is a sign that you care. All his life Foucault concerned himself with those society preferred not to notice: prisoners, people in psychiatric hospitals. Together with others he founded the Prisons Information Group, which published the testimony of prisoners themselves. Hurting for the world is the beginning of attention. You can carry it without letting it extinguish your joy and strength. A little attention to a concrete injustice nearby is already a response.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small, concrete way to help someone near you. And allow yourself one joy today — it isn't a betrayal.

quote.text: Do not think that one has to be sad in order to be militant, even though the thing one is fighting is abominable.
quote.author: Michel Foucault
quote.source: Preface to the English edition of Deleuze and Guattari’s Anti-Oedipus (1977)

rejection.text: The examination, for Foucault, turns a person into a "case": they are assigned scores and a place in a row, and they become a line in a register. School, work, even dating are largely built as endless exams. That is why rejection wounds so deeply: it seems you have been tested and found unfit as a whole. But the decision of another person or an organisation is not an objective verdict; it is a choice by their own criteria and in their own circumstances. These criteria have a history and limits. Foucault reminds us that every scale was invented by someone and leaves something out of the frame. You are more than the result of one exam. A refusal speaks of their criteria, not of your worth.
rejection.practice: Write down the criteria by which you weren't chosen. Then — which of your qualities those criteria didn't measure at all.

abandonment.text: Family and marriage are almost the only forms of connection our society truly recognises, Foucault observed, and he saw the task as inventing new ones: friendships, alliances, networks of mutual care. The fear of being abandoned can be very strong and long-standing — sometimes it reaches back to childhood. It is especially strong when all your support rests on one or two bonds approved by the norm. But life can be richer: friends, communities, mentors, neighbours. The wider the web of care, the less a single parting threatens everything. This doesn't cancel the fear, but it gives you more to lean on. Foucault saw friendship not as a consolation prize but as a full form of life.
abandonment.practice: Draw a map of your connections: who else, besides those closest to you, is in your life? Mark one bond you'd like to strengthen.

unrequited.text: Reciprocity as the norm, "the other half", the happy ending — Foucault taught us to see that even what is most intimate has cultural scripts. Against them an unanswered feeling looks like failure. Unrequited love is a pain full of silence. But your feeling is not a failure; it is an experience that doesn't fit the template. The late Foucault saw life as material to which a person gives shape themselves, as an artist does to a work. Unrequited love can become part of that shape: teach you something about your capacity to feel, about your desires, about what matters to you. It is real, even if there's no answer. Foucault would remind you: no script is obliged to be yours.
unrequited.practice: Sit for five minutes in silence and ask yourself what this love has taught you — about yourself, not about the other person.

humiliation.text: Diogenes, who according to legend was put up for sale at a slave market, answered the question of what he could do with: "Govern men." In his last lectures on the Cynics Foucault loved such scenes: a person refuses to accept the definition imposed on him. Humiliation is one of the deepest wounds: you were stripped of dignity, and it seems everyone saw. Foucault wrote a great deal about how power acts through visibility — from the public punishments of the past to rankings put on display. Humiliation is an act done to you within particular relations of power, not the truth about you. Where there is power there is resistance, and it can begin quietly: by refusing to accept someone else's definition of you.
humiliation.practice: Write down how they tried to define you in the moment of humiliation. Then write one word with which you define yourself.

body_shame.text: The Cynics lived in full view of everyone, hiding nothing, and in his last lecture course Foucault called their life "unconcealed": for them the body was no cause for shame. Dissatisfaction with one's body is a very common and heavy feeling. Foucault showed that the body is not only nature but also a place where norms operate: discipline teaches "docile bodies" how to sit, walk and hold themselves properly, and "biopower" measures and standardises life. Shame about the body is often not your personal judgement but the imprint of such norms. They have a history: in other eras the ideals of the body were quite different. This knowledge doesn't cancel the shame at once, but it helps you hear someone else's voice in it rather than your own truth.
body_shame.practice: Walk around the room the way that's comfortable for you, not "the proper way": belly relaxed, shoulders loose. Notice whose norm is trying to correct you.

illness.text: "What is the matter with you?" — this, according to Foucault, is what an eighteenth-century doctor asked a patient, whereas modern medicine began to ask "Where does it hurt?" In "The Birth of the Clinic" he described this "medical gaze", which sees a person as a case, a set of symptoms and readings. This gaze has saved countless lives, but a patient may feel that they themselves are disappearing behind the diagnosis. Illness is a hard experience: the body lets you down, and familiar life changes; fear, anger, tiredness are legitimate here. You are more than your diagnosis. The late Foucault studied ancient "care of the self", in which care of the body was part of care for one's whole life — thoughts, relationships, habits.
illness.practice: Tell someone close how you are — not about symptoms, but about what you thought, read and felt today. You are not only a case.

pride.text: Alexander the Great offered to grant Diogenes any wish, and Diogenes asked only that he step aside and stop blocking the sun; Foucault analysed this scene as a model of a dignity that needs no one's approval. Pride in what you've done is a good, legitimate feeling: you have accomplished something, and it deserves to be acknowledged. The late Foucault spoke of an "aesthetics of existence" — the idea that life can be built like a work of art, given its own form. Healthy pride is a craftsman's joy at seeing something take shape through his work. It is not a place in a ranking or a victory over others but joy in one's own work. Let yourself be glad.
pride.practice: Step into the sun or towards the light for a minute and stand there, asking no one for approval. Name silently what shape your work has given to your life.

melancholy.text: Black bile, "animal spirits", nerves — in "History of Madness" Foucault traced how doctors of different eras explained melancholy in different ways: the very concept changed its meaning more than once. What today we want to "fix" immediately was understood differently in other times — among other things, as a companion of reflection and fine sensibility. Gentle melancholy is a subtle, sometimes even precious feeling. Foucault paid attention to states that don't fit the image of an always "productive" person. Your gentle melancholy doesn't have to be a problem. You can simply live it as part of your life — quiet and particular. The ancients saw melancholy as the temperament of poets and thinkers, not only as an illness.
melancholy.practice: Spend a few minutes with this mood: by the window, with music, or on a walk. Don't ask it why it has come.
